memories.text: {Their} father, Suresh Rao, taught Kannada and history at the government high school in {hometown} for thirty-one years and retired two years ago. Strict but fair; still corrects everyone's grammar and reads the newspaper aloud at breakfast whether anyone listens or not.

With {their} father the talk is mostly news, marks and money, but once, when the bus was cancelled, he rode {name} forty kilometres on his old Bajaj scooter at five in the morning so {they} would not miss an entrance exam. {They} has never forgotten it.

{Their} mother, Lakshmi, runs the home. Up at five, a rangoli at the door every morning, the best bisi bele bath on the street. She phones every evening around eight, and her first question is always whether {name} has eaten.

{Their} brother {sibling} is 19, in second-year mechanical engineering near {hometown}. Loud, funny, mad about cricket; calls {name} 'boss' and asks for money for shoes more often than for books. {They} still helps him with maths over the phone.

{Their} ajji, the father's mother, lived with the family until she died when {name} was fifteen. She told the same story about a cobra in the paddy field every monsoon and hid chakkuli in a steel box for the grandchildren.

Grew up in a small rented two-room house near the old market in {hometown}, with a guava tree in the yard that {name} and {sibling} were always climbing. The family moved into school staff quarters when {they} was twelve.

At eight, {name} got lost at the Dasara fair in {hometown}. A policeman found {them} two hours later sitting calmly with a balloon seller, eating groundnuts. The family still tells it at every wedding.
Loves the first rain of the season and the smell of wet mud. As children, {name} and {sibling} raced paper boats down the gutter outside the house.
The house rule was home before the street lights came on. {sibling} broke it all the time; {name} almost never did, and was the one sent to fetch him.
Never had a pet. A street dog called Kalu slept outside their gate in {hometown} for years, and {name} saved the leftover chapatis for him.

Went to the same government high school where {their} father taught, so every teacher reported everything home. Good at maths, never learned to like Sanskrit, came second in the district in the tenth standard exams.
Best friend from school is Shruti, now a bank clerk in {hometown}. She is getting married in February and has already made {name} promise to come for all three days.
Best friend from school is Naveen, now a bank clerk in {hometown}. He is getting married in February and has already made {name} promise to come for all three days.

Did a B.E. in computer science at a private engineering college two hours from home, going back every second weekend by KSRTC bus. Shared a hostel room with three others and learned to cook Maggi in an electric kettle.
The closest college friends are Deepa and Kiran. The three of them have a WhatsApp group called 'Backbenchers', mostly memes and trips that get planned and never happen.
Has never been on a plane. The best trip so far was a college trip to Gokarna: the beach at night, sleeping on the sand, Kiran losing a slipper to the waves.
Got the job through campus placement in the final year. The whole street came to the house with sweets, and {their} father told every shopkeeper in the market.
Works as a software test engineer at an IT services company: writes test cases, runs the regression tests before each release, logs bugs for the developers.

Proudest moment at work: in the very first month, found a bug that would have charged customers twice. The team lead mentioned it on the all-hands call and {name} did not sleep that night from excitement.
In the team, gets on best with Farhan, a senior tester who shares his lunch and explains things patiently, and Meena from the developers' side who sends memes about bugs.
Takes the bus to the tech park in Bellandur, about forty minutes, longer through Silk Board. Uses the ride for old film songs or a technology podcast.
On a normal workday: alarm at seven, filter coffee, the bus, stand-up at ten, lunch in the office canteen at one, home by eight if the traffic is kind, then the call from {their} mother.

The flat in HSR Layout is a two-bedroom on the third floor with a small balcony full of the flatmate's plants. Rent is split in half; the landlord lives on the ground floor and complains about the water bill.
The flatmate is Sneha, a colleague from Pune: cheerful, far too talkative in the mornings, makes poha on Sundays and insists they watch a film together at weekends.
The flatmate is Vikram, a colleague from Lucknow: gym every morning, makes egg bhurji on Sundays and insists they watch a cricket match together at weekends.
Started {hobby} at ten, because a neighbour aunty taught it in the evenings for fifty rupees a month. It was the one thing {name} ever did just for {them}self.

Nothing beats {their} mother's ragi mudde with saaru, or holige at Ugadi. In Bengaluru it is office canteen food and the darshini dosa near the flat. Can cook rice, rasam and an omelette, nothing more.
The first time {name} made sambar in the flat {they} forgot the dal. {Their} mother still brings it up on the phone and laughs.
Goes home for Ugadi and Deepavali every year. At Dasara the family sets up a gombe display of dolls three generations old, and since childhood {name}'s job has been arranging the wooden animals.
Birthday is in March. {Their} mother still makes payasam, and {sibling} still forgets until noon.
With the first salary {name} bought {their} mother a Mysore silk saree and {their} father a wristwatch. He still wears it and tells everyone who gave it to him.
Keeps a small notebook of every rupee spent, a habit from {their} father. After rent, the bus pass and what goes home for {sibling}'s fees, there is not much left over.
Kannada at home, English at work, enough Hindi for delivery drivers, and a few Tamil words picked up from the office.
Likes old Dr Rajkumar films because {their} father watches them, and Korean dramas on the phone at night, which {they} would never admit at the office.
Supports RCB like the whole family, out of loyalty more than hope. {name} and {sibling} still argue about whether Kohli or Dravid is the better batsman.
Not very religious. Goes to the Ganesha temple near the flat on some Tuesdays because {their} mother asks, and likes the quiet there more than the prayers.
Hardly on social media. The family WhatsApp group is mostly {their} father's good-morning flower messages. Has an Instagram account with eleven posts, nearly all sunsets.
In Bengaluru the neighbours barely know {name}'s face. In {hometown} every neighbour knew {their} exam results before {they} did.
Wants to move into test automation one day, buy {their} parents a small house of their own, maybe study for a master's abroad. The plan keeps getting pushed to next year.
Wears plain cotton office clothes and owns exactly one pair of good shoes. Shopping is something {sibling} has to drag {them} to.
Has always been the quiet one: the child who finished homework first, the friend who remembers birthdays, the one who says sorry even when it was someone else's fault.
